reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Anal stenosis is pathological narrowing of the anal canal with loss of its normal elasticity, most often an anatomical (cicatricial) narrowing due to fibrous scar replacing pliable anoderm

The commonest cause is overzealous excisional haemorrhoidectomy with excessive removal of anoderm; other causes include chronic fissure, inflammatory bowel disease, radiation, trauma, and chronic laxative-associated changes
Typical symptoms are difficult and painful defecation, thin or pencil-like stools, straining, incomplete evacuation, and bleeding from mucosal splitting
A functional narrowing due to sphincter spasm (as in chronic fissure) must be distinguished from true anatomical stenosis with fibrosis, as management differs
Severity is graded by the calibre achievable on examination and whether an examining finger or instrument passes; examination may require anaesthesia
Mild stenosis often responds to stool bulking, softeners, and dilatation; moderate to severe fibrotic stenosis requires operative correction
Surgical options include internal sphincterotomy for a tight functional element and anoplasty with advancement or island flaps to introduce healthy tissue and widen the canal
Inflammatory or neoplastic causes must be excluded by biopsy before attributing stenosis to benign scarring, particularly when there is no clear surgical history
reference.pathophysiology: Anal stenosis results from replacement of the elastic, pliable anoderm and mucosa of the anal canal by inelastic fibrous scar, or from fixed narrowing due to inflammatory or neoplastic infiltration. After excisional haemorrhoidectomy or other anal surgery, excessive removal of anoderm leaves broad raw areas that heal by scar contracture, drawing the canal into a rigid, narrowed ring. Chronic anal fissure, Crohn disease, tuberculosis, radiation injury, and chronic dermatoses similarly provoke fibrosis and loss of compliance. The narrowed, non-distensible canal obstructs the passage of stool, causing straining, painful defecation, and mucosal splitting; secondary constipation and stool withholding compound the problem, and any residual sphincter spasm further reduces the effective luminal calibre.
additionalDifferentials: Functional anal narrowing from chronic fissure with sphincter spasm
Anal or low rectal carcinoma causing luminal narrowing
Post-inflammatory stricture from lymphogranuloma venereum or other infection
Congenital anal stenosis in younger patients
Rectal stricture from ischaemia or anastomotic scarring
additionalInvestigations: Careful inspection and gentle digital examination to assess calibre and pliability
Examination under anaesthesia when pain precludes adequate assessment
Proctosigmoidoscopy to inspect above the stenosis
Biopsy of the narrowed segment to exclude Crohn disease, infection, or malignancy
Endoanal ultrasound or pelvic MRI where the cause or extent is unclear
Assessment of sphincter function and continence before planning surgery
redFlags: An indurated or ulcerated stricture suggesting malignancy
Stenosis without prior anal surgery, prompting a search for inflammatory or neoplastic causes
Progressive obstruction or inability to pass stool
Associated fistula, abscess, or perianal Crohn features
Bleeding or discharge disproportionate to a benign scar
reference.prognosis: Mild anal stenosis often responds well to conservative measures and dilatation, while moderate to severe fibrotic stenosis generally requires anoplasty, which gives good results in experienced hands; outcomes are poorer and recurrence more likely when the underlying cause, such as Crohn disease or radiation, is ongoing.
pitfalls: Confusing a functional spasm-related narrowing with true fibrotic stenosis and mismanaging it
Attempting forceful dilatation of dense fibrotic stenosis, causing tearing and incontinence
Failing to biopsy an atypical stricture and missing Crohn disease or malignancy
Performing sphincterotomy alone when tissue deficiency requires flap anoplasty
Removing too much anoderm at the index haemorrhoid operation, which is the commonest preventable cause
references: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
Association of Coloproctology of Great Britain and Ireland guidance on benign anorectal disease
Standard coloproctology reference texts on anoplasty and anal stenosis
management: Distinguish functional narrowing from sphincter spasm from true anatomical fibrotic stenosis, as management differs
Treat mild stenosis conservatively with stool bulking agents, softeners, adequate fibre and gentle dilatation
Relax a functional spasm-related narrowing with a topical internal-sphincter relaxant
Correct moderate to severe fibrotic stenosis surgically with anoplasty using flap techniques
Treat any underlying cause such as Crohn disease or radiation injury, which worsens outcome and recurrence
Biopsy the narrowed segment to exclude Crohn disease, infection or malignancy
Assess sphincter function and continence before planning operative correction
